newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: COMMONWEALTH GAMES CHIEF RESIGNS AFTER CRICITISM.
newsitem.headline: COMMONWEALTH GAMES CHIEF RESIGNS AFTER CRICITISM.

text.p: The executive chairman of the 1998 Commonwealth Games organising committee resigned on Monday after being criticised by two cabinet ministers over preparations for the event.
Retired-General Hashim Mohamed Ali told a news conference he had sent a letter of resignation on Monday to acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

"I personally sent the resignation letter to the office of acting Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim this morning," an emotional Hashim said after meeting Youth and Sports Minister Muhyiddin Yassin.
Muhyiddin and Culture, Arts and Tourism Minister Sabbaruddin Chik had criticised the organising committee for failing to publicise what will be the biggest sporting event ever held in Malaysia.
Sabbaruddin was especially blunt, accusing committee executives of being more interested in travelling first class on overseas trips than in discharging their duties.

"I am very disappointed and surprised at the criticisms hurled at Sukom 98 Berhad (the company organising the games) as reported in the press," said Hashim, a former defence forces chief and the brother-in-law of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad.
Hashim said the criticisms had demoralised his staff.
The national news agency Bernama quoted Muhyiddin as saying he was stunned by Hashim's announcement.
"I was shocked because this meeting (with Hashim on Monday) was only to hear a briefing on Sukom 98 Berhad's operations with only 452 days to go before the prestigious event," he said.

Kuala Lumpur will stage the biggest ever Commonwealth Games with 15 sports expected to attract 6,000 athletes and team officials from 69 countries. A total of 3,300 athletes contested 10 sports at the 1994 Games in Victoria, Canada.

Just last month, Malaysia was brushing off comments from Arthur Tunstall, the Australian Commonwealth Games secretary-general, who said Kuala Lumpur used "the power of money" to win the right to stage the games.
He later apologised, saying his remarks had been misconstrued.
Kuala Lumpur beat Adelaide in 1992 to become the first Asian country to host the Games, scheduled for September 11-21 next year.

Some 100,000 visitors are expected for the Games and a massive building programme in and around the Malaysian capital includes new hotels, a $3.5 billion new airport, an overhead rail transit system and other transport projects.
Malaysia is also spending more than one billion ringgit ($397.6 million) to build a 100,000-seat stadium and other state-of-the-art venues for the event.
Sukom 98 has a 310 million ringgit ($123.3 million) budget for the Games which it hopes to fund through corporate sponsorship.
